name: T. E. Hulme
credit: T. E. Hulme, 1912 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Thomas Ernest Hulme was an English philosopher, critic and translator, best known for introducing Henri Bergson's thought to English readers and for his essays on art and "classical" against "romantic" attitudes, collected after his death as Speculations (1924).

In 1908–09 he gathered the circle of poets around the Poets' Club who met in London to talk about a poetry of hard, exact images, a group often seen as the forerunner of Imagism. Ezra Pound printed Hulme's five poems as an appendix, "The Complete Poetical Works of T. E. Hulme", to his Ripostes (1912).
Hulme enlisted in the Honourable Artillery Company at the outbreak of the First World War and was killed in action near Nieuport, Belgium, on 28 September 1917.

poems.title: Autumn
poems.author: T. E. Hulme
poems.collection: The Complete Poetical Works of T. E. Hulme (1912)
poems.text:
A touch of cold in the Autumn night--
I walked abroad,
And saw the ruddy moon lean over a hedge
Like a red-faced farmer.
I did not stop to speak, but nodded,
And round about were the wistful stars
With white faces like town children.

poems.title: Mana Aboda
poems.author: T. E. Hulme
poems.collection: The Complete Poetical Works of T. E. Hulme (1912)
poems.text:
Beauty is the marking-time, the stationary vibration,
the feigned ecstasy of an arrested impulse unable to
reach its natural end.

Mana Aboda, whose bent form
  The sky in archèd circle is,
  Seems ever for an unknown grief to mourn.
Yet on a day I heard her cry:
"I weary of the roses and the singing poets--
Josephs all, not tall enough to try."

poems.title: Above the Dock
poems.author: T. E. Hulme
poems.collection: The Complete Poetical Works of T. E. Hulme (1912)
poems.text:
Above the quiet dock in mid night,
Tangled in the tall mast's corded height,
Hangs the moon. What seemed so far away
Is but a child's balloon, forgotten after play.

poems.title: The Embankment
poems.author: T. E. Hulme
poems.collection: The Complete Poetical Works of T. E. Hulme (1912)
poems.text:
(The fantasia of a fallen gentleman on a cold, bitter night.)

Once, in finesse of fiddles found I ecstasy,
In the flash of gold heels on the hard pavement.
Now see I
That warmth's the very stuff of poesy.
Oh, God, make small
The old star-eaten blanket of the sky,
That I may fold it round me and in comfort lie.

poems.title: Conversion
poems.author: T. E. Hulme
poems.collection: The Complete Poetical Works of T. E. Hulme (1912)
poems.text:
Lighthearted I walked into the valley wood
In the time of hyacinths,
Till beauty like a scented cloth
Cast over, stifled me. I was bound
Motionless and faint of breath
By loveliness that is her own eunuch.

Now pass I to the final river
Ignominiously, in a sack, without sound,
As any peeping Turk to the Bosphorus.
